title: What’s with all the Brits joining Alpha School?
author: Mark Goodrich
summary: Mark Goodrich responds to Peps McCrea's announcement that he is joining Alpha School's learning-science team, noting that eight of the fourteen people profiled on the school's site are British or Irish. He summarises Alpha neutrally as a model in which children use AI apps for two morning hours, supervised by "guides" rather than teachers, with life skills in the afternoon. Goodrich does not mock the hires, accepts that educators are underpaid and that expertise inside Alpha is better than none, but lists four concerns. These are that pay makes intellectual honesty hard, that the scientists appear siloed from the wider programme, that experimenting on privileged children limits the research, and that "crushing academics" in two hours reflects values at odds with those the hires have espoused. He closes worrying about how Alpha would respond if its own experts said the core premise was wrong.
points: Alpha's apps are described by its own new hire as "okay" rather than amazing, which suggests extrinsic motivation, not the software, is its real engine.
Employees paid handsomely by the institution they evaluate face a built-in threat to intellectual honesty, illustrated by the tension with David Yeager's intrinsic-motivation research.
The learning scientists seem confined to the two-hour academic block and not to the Bootcamp or life-skills afternoons.
Research on the richest students tells us little about what works for disadvantaged ones, which is where Engelmann looked.
Treating academics as something to clear away in two hours is a statement of values, not just a scheduling choice.
quotes: The model for crushing academics is children using lots of AI apps and personalised learning with no teachers as such but rather adults who are described as “guides”.4 The guides are supposed to motivate and support children but not actually teach them which is all left to the apps.
First, it seems clear that the current apps are fairly basic and Alpha’s “secret sauce” is actually amped-up extrinsic motivation.
It’s going to be hard to be intellectually honest about an institution that is paying you very handsomely.
They can tinker away with the apps but what’s going to happen if the “learning scientists” discover something which they think is fundamentally broken with the Alpha model?
Whatever you might think about the methods Zig Engelmann eventually arrived at, he was surely right to look to develop teaching for the most disadvantaged rather than the most advantaged.
Nothing in what Alpha has done to date suggests that they care much for the poorest in society or are looking for solutions to reduce educational disadvantage.
Speaking from my own perspective, the whole idea of trying to get academics out of the way in a 2 hour block to free up time is very far from the values I would like to see in education.

Everything about Alpha School is so fixated on the idea that you can make superb academic progress in 2 hours, how would they respond if their own “learning scientists” told them that it was the wrong approach?
